speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A number of questions have been raised following her acquittal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They centre around: how did the Police and Attorney-General's Chambers or AGC handle the case?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How should the State Court Judgment be assessed, given the High Court’s views?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There has been much attention on this case.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This fundamental issue is at the heart of many of the questions that have been raised.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that question is of central importance to us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If that principle is compromised, then Singapore is compromised.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a basic duty of the Government to ensure that that principle is upheld and I take it very seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And so it is good that we deal with this, with the questions that have been asked.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will start first with the case: the investigations, the conduct of trial and the specific questions which have arisen, relating to the case – it will be Part 1 of my Statement.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will then move on to Part 2 which will deal with the fundamental questions as I have put them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And in Part 3, I will deal with the questions that Members of Parliament have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not going to be a short speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And at the end of Part 1, it may be appropriate to take a break and then come back for Parts 2 and 3.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the end of Part 1, but certainly by end of Part 3, we will probably know what is happening in the US.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Court, the following was said – and I am setting out what was said, not commenting whether it is true or false.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the years, the family’s possessions went missing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: LML gave examples such as a bag he bought from Tokyo, his jogging shoes, a number of Longchamp bags.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He suspected Ms Liyani of stealing but did not take action as he could not be sure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A specially designed power bank from France, that was gifted to LML, “disappeared” a few days after he had received it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Subsequent investigations showed that this may have happened in May 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By then, the only occupants in the house were LML, his wife Ng Lai Peng – whom I will refer to as NLP – and Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Though some others may have had access to the house, LML then decided to terminate Ms Liyani’s employment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this context – and I should add and I will come back to this later – subsequent investigations also showed that earlier, in late 2015, the Liews were looking to replace Ms Liyani because they thought she was stealing things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In September 2016, they decided to terminate her employment and told the maid agency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once a replacement helper was available, they decided to let Ms Liyani go.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: LML was travelling, he told his wife to arrange for people to be around and serve the notice of termination.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Karl told Ms Liyani they were sending her back.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani asked for boxes to pack her things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She packed them with some assistance from the Liews’ other employees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She sealed one box with tape and wrote her address on it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other two boxes were sealed by two other employees of LML.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Karl agreed to pay for the boxes to be sent back to Indonesia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani left the house with the employment agent and returned to Indonesia that night.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The replacement helper commenced her employment at LML’s house on the same day, 28 October 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When he got home, Karl told his wife Heather Lim – and I will refer to her as Heather – about what had happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Heather told him that the boxes should not be sent back without knowing what was inside them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 29 October 2016, in the afternoon, NLP, Karl and Heather opened the boxes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They said they found items which belonged to them which they had not seen for years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They spent about two hours going through the items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: LML returned to Singapore some time on 29 October 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He spent a short time going through the contents of the boxes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 4 November 2016, a Police Gazette was issued.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will come back to this later and deal with the Police Gazette or PG.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 2 December 2016 at about 9 pm, Ms Liyani returned to Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She was arrested at the airport based on the PG.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani said in her statement to the Police, that she came back to visit a friend and go sightseeing thereafter, and she planned to return to Indonesia before going to Hong Kong to work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Later in Court, she said that she, in fact, returned to Singapore to look for her agent and seek employment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When she was arrested, some items were found on her.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are listed in Annex 1, Table A to my Statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Liews said these were also stolen items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These items were seized and subsequently included in the charges against her.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now deal with how the investigations were conducted by the Police, how AGC assessed the case and proceeded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: LML had lodged a Police report, as I said earlier, on 30 October.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police report stated that over the years, the family's belongings had gone missing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They terminated her employment on 28 October and they found some of the items packed in her boxes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Initial investigations showed that Ms Liyani had left Singapore on 28 October itself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: LML had set out in his Police statement the items which he said had been stolen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The items were, according to LML, found amongst Ms Liyani's belongings in the boxes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police needed to trace Ms Liyani to investigate further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where there is reason to suspect that an arrestable offence has been committed, the Police will try to find the alleged offender and, if appropriate, arrest the person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the person is at a known address, the Police can go and interview the person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is no known address or if the person is believed to have gone overseas, then a PG will be issued.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And so, a PG was issued in this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani was believed to have gone overseas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 2 December, at about 9 pm, as I said earlier, she was arrested at the airport.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 3 December, the Police went to the Liews' houses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the three boxes had been moved there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Karl told the Police the items in the box were his.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police were told that the box containing Karl's items had been brought back to his home.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The box contained an assortment of items – clothing, bedding, kitchen ware, utensils.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These photos were used in recording the various statements taken subsequently.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police were told that the two boxes had remained there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: NLP had recovered some items from the boxes – jewellery, accessories, watches, Gucci sunglasses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were said to belong to LML's daughter, Ms May Liew, and I will refer to her as May.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These items are set out in Annex 2.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police did not seize all the items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Items found in those boxes are set out in Annex 1, Table B.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They took statements from Ms Liyani, the Liews and other witnesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now set out how AGC proceeded in coming to the charging decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When AGC receives a file from a law enforcement agency, the prosecutors will assess whether a charge is appropriate and what action, if any, should be taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The assessment and decision are usually cleared by a Director.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Files are typically cleared at the Director level, not usually brought up to a higher management – by which I mean the Deputy Chief Prosecutor, the Chief Prosecutor, the Deputy Attorney-General or Attorney-General, or AG – unless they involve more serious or sensitive crimes or where AG's consent to prosecute is expressly required.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It went through the same routine and the charging decision was cleared at the Director level.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The events leading up to the charging decision were as follows.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such theft files are routine matters handled by AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The file was reviewed by two Deputy Public Prosecutors or DPPs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They asked the Police to investigate a number of further points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The police did that and returned the file to AGC with further findings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They sought further clarifications, and the file was then sent back to the Police for further investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, they sent the file back to AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This back and forth between the Police and AGC is again normal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In many cases, DPPs will look at the material and ask further questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because of the system in AGC, depending on which officer is on duty, it would be different DPPs who look at the same file and that was what happened here as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From the Police and AGC's perspective, this was handled as a routine theft case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was no attempt by anyone to influence them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Police report was filed and the matter was dealt with as such reports are usually dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In contrast, based on what AGC saw, Ms Liyani gave answers which raised many questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani claimed that she had found some jewellery in May's trash.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: May stated that she would never throw jewellery away.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She would give unwanted jewellery to the Salvation Army or friends.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC's assessment was that the evidence of May was more believable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani also claimed that she had found items such as a Prada bag, two Apple iPhones, a pair of Gucci sunglasses in the trash.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC did not find this to be credible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The list of items that Ms Liyani said she found in the trash are in Annex 3 and those are the photographs that have been circulated to Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In her first statement dated 3 December 2016, Ms Liyani was asked how she came into possession of male clothing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She said the clothing belonged to her employer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She said she took the clothing because the clothes were small.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She assumed the employer's son Karl would not want the clothes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She did not ask Karl whether she could take the clothes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She admitted to taking the pieces of male clothing in early 2015.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I admit that I took it without informing my employer or her husband".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And she also said, "I only admit to taking the 10 to 15 men's clothing belonging to my employer's husband without consent" and "I did not steal any other items." Her statement that she did not steal any other items is also very significant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prima facie on the statements, this would appear to be theft.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC assessed the case based on this and other material.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should add that under cross-examination in Court, Ms Liyani said she was only given permission to take these items if Karl did not want them, but she did not ask Karl, meaning she just took the items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani also gave contradictory accounts to the Police on several other items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These inconsistencies are set out in Annex 4.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will highlight two instances of inconsistencies as illustrations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One Vacheron Constantin watch and a Swatch watch – in her statement dated 4 December, Ms Liyani said these watches were gifts from a friend.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, in a later statement of 29 May 2017, she said she found these watches in May's trash.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A pair of Gucci sunglasses – in her statement dated 4 December 2016, she said this was a gift from LML's previous helper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a later statement of May 2017, she said she found it in her room at LML's home when she first started working for LML.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should add, later in Court, Ms Liyani was asked about these contradictions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Her explanations are also set out in the table at Annex 4.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At that stage, the Liews' position was that the items were theirs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two reasons: one, it appeared that Ms Liyani had stolen many items, including some seemingly expensive items; and two, it appeared that she had been stealing for years and it was not an impulsive spur-of-the-moment decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the questions for Members in this House, in this case, is, on what I have set out – what material evidence did Police and AGC have?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Was there a basis for AGC's view that the case ought to be prosecuted?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why I have set out this material in some detail, so that Members can assess for themselves the basis for the decisions that the Police and AGC came to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now move on to the trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The DPPs who conducted the trial were different from the DPPs who had previously been involved in the charging process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani was represented by counsel assigned under the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, or CLAS, for both the trial and the appeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The trial judge found serious inconsistencies in Ms Liyani's evidence between what she said in Court and her previous statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Court noted that Ms Liyani had various versions in relation to specific items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani said different things in her statement compared with what she said in evidence in chief in Court and then sometimes, changed her version under cross-examination.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have earlier referred to Annex 4, which sets out these inconsistencies and also her explanations for these inconsistencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Court found Ms Liyani's evidence on some items to be implausible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, the two old white iPhones – she said she picked up the two phones from a rubbish bag.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These were iPhone 4 models, probably about six years old as of 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Court preferred the Liews' evidence that they would not discard old mobile phones as they were used as spare phones or as hard drives to keep photographs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Jewellery – Ms Liyani said that most of the jewellery was picked from May's rubbish in 2011 or 2012 and she did not seek permission to take them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: May identified the items as hers and provided circumstances of how and why she purchased them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Court preferred May's version as it was more detailed and she came across as honest and forthright.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani said that a purple Prada bag and Gucci sunglasses with red stains were found in a rubbish bag.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Court accepted Heather's evidence that these items were never discarded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The trial judge said the modus operandi of Ms Liyani was to take a variety of items from different family members, thinking that this would go unnoticed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, there had been a break in the chain of custody of the items, which were said to have been stolen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition, the High Court also expressed doubts about the credibility of the prosecution witnesses, in particular, Karl.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It also expressed doubts on the extent to which Ms Liyani's statements given to the Police should be used against her.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should say this – as a rule, we do not comment in detail on Court decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, we deal with specific issues that can arise from decisions or comments; and when decisions raised broader questions, then, this House has discussed the relevant judgments, like the City Harvest case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, the High Court's comments have given rise to the questions I have referred to earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These questions require us to go back and carefully analyse the judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is difficult to discuss the law enforcement and legal processes, here in Parliament, based on the High Court's comments without a proper understanding of the comments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also cannot make an assessment of whether the comments require us to change any of our current processes without looking carefully at the relevant parts of the judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I will therefore be looking at parts of the High Court judgment to give the Government's views on them, and based on that, I will set up what gaps there were in the investigations, conduct of the trial and also say what more could or should have been done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as we do this, let me make three points clear and reiterate what I have said earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the High Court's decision is final, on the acquittal; there is no appeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, I am making no comment as to whether the High Court's decision can be relied upon, or whether the Judge’s comments can be relooked at in other proceedings, for example, in any proceedings that Ms Liyani or others are or may be involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are Rules of Evidence relating to these matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, in this case, we have had to deal with the questions raised, whether there were or are any systemic issues with our law enforcement processes, and for that purpose, we have to discuss the Judgment, the Government’s view and also look at some additional factual material, which we came to know of after the Judgment was delivered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This exercise is not one of reopening the Judgment, and I should emphasise that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are going into detail only because it is necessary for the purposes I have explained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us start with, first, the motive point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Judge said at paragraph 52 of the Judgment, and I quote, "the Police report was made just two days after Parti made explicit to two members of Liew’s family of her intention to lodge a complaint to the MOM about being required to work illegally at Karl’s residence at 39 CL and at Karl’s office" There are two points here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And second, what was the Liews’ motive in making the allegations?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it is shown that there is a reasonable doubt that the Liews had an improper motive, then what they say about Ms Liyani and the theft of items could become questionable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The evidence is that as Ms Liyani was packing her things on 28 October 2016, she said she was going to complain to MOM.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She did not say what she was going to complain to MOM about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court, in fact, said this threat by Ms Liyani on 28 October 2016 to lodge a complaint with MOM was, I quote, "most critical".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the Court then said the Liews filed the "urgent" Police report on 30 October 2016 to ensure that Ms Liyani’s return would be prevented, and so that Ms Liyani cannot file a complaint to MOM.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, the Court said that the termination of her employment was sudden, so that Ms Liyani would not have time to complain to MOM.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will deal with all these three observations that the Court made because it is these observations on the Liews’ motive which have primarily led to questions in this case on whether there was any improper influence by LML on the agencies, which is the question centrally before us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When Ms Liyani said on 28 October 2016 that she was going to complain to MOM, what was she referring to?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex 5 sets out what Ms Liyani seems to have said and this is based on subsequent investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She thus seemed to have actually said more than what was in evidence in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex 5 also sets out why this part of what she said was not in evidence in the State Courts and I will come back to this later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How and why was this subsequent evidence obtained?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the High Court's decision was issued, there were internal reviews, as announced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC also directed the Police to conduct further investigations into whether any offences had been committed by the Liews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This information that I have set out, and other information, was obtained in the course of those investigations, which arose from the High Court's decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I emphasise that, as a result of the High Court's comments, further investigations were conducted against the Liews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was in the course of those investigations that this information came out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As stated earlier, the evidence is that LML had been thinking of terminating Ms Liyani’s employment for some time, prior to October 2016, because he suspected Ms Liyani of stealing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The further investigations, conducted after the High Court's decision, show that NLP told the maid agency by end of 2015 that she wanted to get a new helper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She told the maid agency that she suspected Ms Liyani of stealing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She went to the agency a few times to review bio-data of possible replacement helpers, but NLP did not make a firm decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometime after LML received the power bank in May 2016, it disappeared.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: LML then decided to terminate Ms Liyani’s employment and told NLP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: NLP visited the agency in September 2016 and chose a replacement helper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: According to LML, he had agreed with NLP that Ms Liyani would only be dismissed once a replacement was found.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on what the maid agent has said to the Police, the new helper arrived in Singapore on 25 October 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On 28 October 2016, after Ms Liyani was told that her employment was terminated, Ms Liyani said "I want to complain because you gave me too short notice".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the maid agents who was present then, confirms this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He says, after Ms Liyani was told that her employment was terminated, Ms Liyani "shouted that she wanted to complain to MOM about the short notice of termination".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani did not say that she wanted to complain to MOM about anything else.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As can be seen, this is quite different from the inference that the High Court had made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the High Court understandably and naturally went on the basis of the evidence and the submissions made to it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court did not have the benefit of this additional evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as I have said, our purpose is not to reopen the High Court’s findings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First time was at 49 CL when Ms Liyani first said that she wanted to complain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the second time was at the agent’s office before they left for the airport.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prosecution, in general, puts forward the evidence it needs for the charges and to deal with the points that the Defence says it is going to make or raise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When a new point gets raised during the trial, Prosecution will have to assess how to proceed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, the matter was raised when witnesses were on the stand and in Submissions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prosecution did not see a need to deal with the issue by bringing in new evidence for the reasons set out in Annex 5.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex 5 is a Note prepared by AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I asked them to give me a Note, setting out how this point on Motive was handled in Court and the position that AGC took.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How a trial is handled, what evidence is led, is a matter for the lawyers involved to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the other side raises a new point, do you deal with it by going back and checking if there is further evidence or do you treat it as irrelevant, or do you deal with it in Submissions?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It really depends on the situation and the facts, the Counsel’s assessment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we are not here discussing the specifics of how the trial was conducted, and whether how it was conducted was right or wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My task before this House is to set out what happened, what we have found out since the High Court's Judgment and, based on that, examine whether there are any systemic issues, and whether there was any influence-peddling.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I also emphasise Members must take this further evidence in its proper context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But since this has come up during the further investigations as to whether the Liews committed an offence, I am duty bound to set this out in this House because it is in my possession.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I cannot come here and go through the facts without telling you that we have this further information which only came about because the further investigations into the Liews’ conduct was directed by AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now deal with the second point that the High Court made, that the Liews filed the Police report to try and prevent Ms Liyani from making an MOM complaint.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court made the same point to Defence counsel during the hearing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She does not even have to be in Singapore to do that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If an MOM complaint was a key concern, filing a Police Report and having Police investigations is possibly a sure way for such a complaint to be raised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Should Ms Liyani attempt to return, Police investigations would also require her to remain in Singapore, once again offering her a further opportunity to pursue an MOM complaint against the Liews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court has also said that LML’s reasons for filing the Police report were "curious".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: LML had stated that he was lodging the Police report "for record purposes as he was afraid that her boyfriends might cause a nuisance or break into   apartment".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Looking at it in this House, Ms Liyani had left and had asked for three boxes to be sent to her.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Liews had opened the boxes and were not going to send them to her.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They said they found items belonging to them in the boxes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They also said that they were concerned that Ms Liyani's boyfriends in Singapore might try to retrieve the items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the circumstances, is it understandable that a Police Report is filed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it possible to think that Ms Liyani or persons acting on her behalf will ask what happened to the items and may accuse the Liews?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I put forward these points on filing the Police Report because for our purposes, in this context, the question is not whether the High Court is right or wrong but, rather, the question is how did the AGC and Police proceed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is there anything so obviously wrong about the filing of the Police Report that should have been apparent to the Police and the AGC?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the central question; not whether the High Court was right, wrong; State Court, who says what.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Did AGC and Police proceed in good faith, based on the material before them and what was before them?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am putting these points across, so that Members can place themselves in the shoes of Police and AGC and think of these points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is for the same reason that I will go through some of the other points which I will come to, but I may not keep repeating these points about why I am going into detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as long as Members understand the purpose of much of what I have said, and will say, the detail that I am setting out is broadly to help understand what was the basis on which Police and AGC proceeded in this case – did they have good reason to proceed, what did they know before the trial – and we are looking at that to see whether, systemically, anything was wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third point that the High Court made relates to the termination of Ms Liyani's employment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court said the termination of Ms Liyani's employment was sudden, since there was no evidence of items that had gone missing in the period around 28 October 2016 which necessitated the "immediate and sudden termination" of Ms Liyani's employment when LML was overseas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, the High Court said this sudden termination was less likely to be because of items that went missing "over the years" and more likely to be due to fear of Ms Liyani's complaint to MOM.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have set out the way this point came up and how this point had been dealt with in evidence at the trial and what subsequent investigations showed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police did not go into this earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was no reason for the Police to believe that the termination was for reasons other than the alleged theft.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now deal with a couple more points on the motive issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court used different terminologies to describe the Liews' motive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It said "reason to believe", "reasonable doubt", "an improper motive", "the improper motive", it referred to "the existence of an improper motive".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is not clear, was there only a reasonable doubt that the Liews had an improper motive, or is the Court saying the Liews actually, in fact, had an improper motive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it will be a fair assumption that the High Court intended to say that there was a reasonable doubt and not that in fact, it found, that there was an improper motive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It means that the High Court says there is a reasonable doubt as to whether the Liews had an improper motive, and not that they in fact had an improper motive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court also rejected the allegation that the whole of the Liew family were acting in collusion, based on the improper motive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This view on motive appears to have considerably influenced the High Court in assessing the witnesses' credibility as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court said this at various points in the judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is the first reason why Ms Liyani was acquitted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now come to the second major reason for the High Court acquitting Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The items which were recovered from the boxes, are set out in Annex 1, Table B.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The items which were recovered from Ms Liyani, upon her arrest, are set out in Annex 1, Table A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The break in the chain of custody applies to the items recovered from the boxes, and not the items seized from Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you refer to the items in the boxes – I have set out the facts earlier – the High Court found that there had been a break in the chain of the items from 29 October 2016 when they were found in the boxes by the Liews, to 3 December 2016 when the Police visited the scene.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Liews were also using the items in the boxes during this period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court therefore said the case of theft is not proven because it cannot be proven that Ms Liyani took them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There could have been interference when the boxes were with the Liews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These items can be classified into two categories: one, items which Ms Liyani admitted to packing in the boxes, or otherwise admitted to taking; and two, items which she did not specifically admit to packing into her boxes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where Ms Liyani admitted to packing the items, or taking the items, then it really does not matter whether there was a chain of custody, or whether that chain of custody was broken, because she clearly intended to take these items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Looking at the facts, the High Court's view that there was a break in the chain of custody is understandable in respect of these items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A fourth charge relates to items in Heather’s possession, comprised solely of items seized from Ms Liyani, including a Prada bag and a pair of Gucci sunglasses with red stains, when she came back from Jakarta.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The break in chain of custody does not apply to these items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have gone through the break in chain of custody in some detail because this was the second major reason the Judge gave.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But more importantly, because it relates directly to what the Police did, or did not do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For Members' understanding, it is useful to know which items are affected by the break in the chain, which items are not so affected, and that several items are not affected by the break in the chain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is because there has been a misunderstanding amongst some, that all the items are affected by the break in the chain of custody.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have set out at Annex 6 how the issue of chain of custody affected the various items in the charges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court had doubts about the Liews' credibility, in particular, it highlighted Karl's evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It noted the following points about Karl's evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, Karl did not clearly identify some pieces of clothing in the second charge, such as a black dress as having been in his possession.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Karl also had difficulties with some of the other items of clothing, like a cream Polo t-shirt and a red blouse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court found Karl's claim that he wore women's t-shirts suspect – I am using the High Court's words.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Karl testified that a Gucci wallet and a Braun Buffel wallet belonged to him and were gifts from his family.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, none of his family members could recall gifting him those specific items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: High Court disbelieved his evidence and thought he was being untruthful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court disbelieved that a Helix watch was a gift from LML.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Karl agreed that a pink knife that he had earlier said he had purchased before 2002, was likely manufactured after that date.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court said this affected Karl's credibility and his claim to ownership.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court disbelieved Karl’s evidence that he had bought a bedsheet in the UK, from Habitat and that High Court said he had, I quote, "fabricated his testimony".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The bedsheet had the same pattern as a quilt cover which had an IKEA label.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Karl's wife, Heather, also testified that she had never seen the bedsheet in her room or on her bed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Gerald Genta watch – Karl said initially the value was $25,000.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Defence experts put the then current value at $500, given its state: a chronograph pusher was missing, date malfunctioned and the strap needed replacing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are two issues here: whether Karl's evidence can be relied upon to convict Ms Liyani; and two, whether Karl was being dishonest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court chose to give little weight to what he said and said he was unreliable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given that Ms Liyani's liberty was at stake, I think many lawyers will understand that the whole of Karl's evidence was disregarded, as the High Court did.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point – was Karl being dishonest?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Statements have been taken from Karl on the following points: whether the items highlighted by the High Court had been in his possession; his explanations for his inconsistencies during trial, regarding these items; the investigations have been completed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before I move on from the issue of credibility, let me say a few words about both Ms Liyani and the Liews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said before, I am making these points to provide better context to deal with the questions that we are discussing and to better understand the basis on which Police and AGC proceeded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I want to be brief because there are on-going investigations and proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the benefit of Members, we have prepared a table which sets out the different items; the evidence, including the inconsistencies in evidence of both Ms Liyani and the Liews, and the explanations, the State Court's views; and the High Court’s views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Broadly speaking, Ms Liyani gave a number of reasons for her inconsistent answers: one, she did not understand the questions posed; two, the interviewers did not understand her answers or did not record her answers accurately; for example, when she admitted to taking the 10 to 15 items of male clothings; three, she meant to say something different from what was recorded in her statement; four, she was shown unclear or blurry photos of some items, so she might have given the wrong answers because she could not recognise the items properly; five, there was a black bag in her room, which contained items left behind by the previous helper of the Liews' which the previous helper did not want, and the items from that bag may have been packed into the boxes inadvertently by those who were helping Ms Liyani to pack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the Liews, Karl gave inconsistent answers in some areas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in some instances, the testimony of one of the Liews was either contradicted, or at variance with the evidence of another family member.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There was some debate on the value of some items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Defence also put in some articles on Dumpster Diving, suggesting expensive items, like branded bags do get disposed of in the trash in Singapore and thus, Ms Liyani could have picked them up from the trash cans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The argument is that Ms Liyani could have found, for example, the Prada bag and the jewellery which May says were hers, in the trash.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are various aspects of Ms Liyani’s evidence which prima facie, raise scepticism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were inconsistencies in many of her answers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Answers changed from one statement to another and from her statements to her evidence in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Several aspects of her evidence in Court also raise questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Items which were said to be found in trash, for example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will leave Members to reach their own views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am giving you this summary to let you know how the Police and AGC assessed the matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, of course, when they did so, they did not have the benefit of her evidence in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And for other reasons, relating to the reliability of Ms Liyani's statements, if there were issues with the statement-taking, then that affects the question of whether there were in fact inconsistencies in her statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Moving on to the Liews, there are many aspects of Karl's conduct and evidence – some of which I have dealt with – which are highly unsatisfactory, which raise scepticism based on what he said at trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He appeared not to be a credible witness.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Filing a Police report, making claims on items need to be taken seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not have to be a comprehensive account, but it must be done with careful consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Looking at the evidence, the impression one gets is that there seems to have been a cavalier attitude on the part of the Liews in the way some items were identified as belonging to them and in the way values were ascribed to some items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is natural to expect that you will know and take your duties seriously when you file a Police report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Be careful in what you say and do, commensurate with your knowledge and experience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you claim an item, you make sure it is yours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you ascribe a value, make sure you have a basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Questions do arise about how one or more of the Liews have conducted themselves on these and other aspects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is more I would have liked to have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have not made any comments about honesty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have been somewhat restrained because of the investigations and I have referred to a statement that will be issued tonight as a result of the investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this context again, the key issue for us is to go back to the Police and AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They had the statements from the Prosecution witnesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They did not know that Karl or others would be inconsistent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The inconsistent evidence from Karl and other witnesses came at trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It happens quite – I would not say quite frequently – but not infrequently.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends on the cross-examiner, it depends on how much they had thought about it and other reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it happens often enough, in civil cases as well as criminal cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is nothing unusual about that either.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now deal with the fourth reason given by the High Court in acquitting Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A total of five Police statements were recorded from Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She gave the first four statements in Malay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She gave her fifth statement with the aid of a Bahasa Indonesia interpreter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 22(4) of the CPC requires a written statement to be read over to the person who gives it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the person does not understand English, it must be read over in a language that he or she understands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court also said that this was not a "flagrant violation".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They remained as evidence, though the Court will decide what weight to give to it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, the Police officers believed in good faith that Ms Liyani understood Malay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She had worked in Singapore for over 20 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The recorder asked Ms Liyani in Malay whether she wished to give her statement in Malay or in Bahasa Indonesia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no significant difference between Malay and Bahasa Indonesia in the asking of that question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She did not ask for an interpreter during the recording of her statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The recorder testified in Court that he was able to communicate with her, without any difficulties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court recognised that she understood some Malay, though the extent of her understanding was unclear to the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court said that differences in the two languages could create reasonable doubt on the accuracy of the statements recorded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, the Police believed in good faith that Ms Liyani understood Malay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Police accept that there are differences between Bahasa Indonesia and our Malay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in specific words, some words, they could mean different things, in the context of this case and that can make a difference if Ms Liyani did not know the different meanings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 22(4)(b) of the CPC makes clear the key requirement is that the interviewee understands what is being said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A Bahasa Indonesia interpreter was provided in recording her final statement and when the charges were served on her.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The final statement dealt with the majority of the areas covered in the previous statements recorded from Ms Liyani and the items in the charges that were tendered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, on that basis, her final statement is not affected by any issues relating to interpretation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At trial, Ms Liyani said that she may not have understood some aspects of the final statement because it was read back in a mixture of Malay and Bahasa Indonesia, and that the interpreter was "talking too fast".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The statement reflected that it had been read back in Bahasa Indonesia, and Ms Liyani had affirmed that to be correct and true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now, Sir, deal with the specific issues that have been pointed out by the High Court in respect of the Police investigations, AGC and the State Court's judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have earlier set out the facts that the Police had, after the investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When there is a complaint of theft, Police need to be fair to both the employer and the domestic worker.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It means Police will have to investigate properly when there is a prima facie case and let AGC decide whether to prosecute.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If as a rule, Police take no action and if it is known that Police would not take action, Members can work out what the consequences will be for themselves, as in you can think and work out the consequences what such an approach will mean.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to approach this with the perspective of both the 250,000 foreign domestic workers, to be fair to them but also to the 200,000-odd families who employ them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they believe that their employees have stolen or done something wrong, what are they supposed to do?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could be any one of these families.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have to be very careful in how we deal with this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am referring to 2016, for illustrative purposes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they were handled by about 1,100 IOs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, theft as servant cases involving foreign domestic workers, roughly one every 1.5 days or two every three days.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, three in four not prosecuted; one in four prosecuted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is based on investigations and assessment by Police and AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And also, even when there is some case but if it is not clear, sometimes, warnings are given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained earlier the reasons for the prosecution in this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The case was handled by the Police like they handle any routine theft case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was handled by the IO and cleared by his immediate supervisor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I say IO when he was out, one or other IOs did handle it as well, but at the level of the investigation officer, cleared by his immediate supervisor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This was a routine matter, cleared via normal channels.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The matter was not considered or brought to the attention of anyone senior, at any time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Except that many of us came to know about it, when it was reported in the media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the question is, was there a clear, prima facie case for the Police to investigate?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If any Member feels that Police should not have investigated, I would be happy to hear and understand their perspective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court commented on investigative processes, pointed out three aspects, which it felt were deficient.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The scene should have been visited by the Police close to the time of the Police report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This was a lapse, which affected some, but not all, of the items in the charges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In terms of the acquittal, the High Court also acquitted Ms Liyani in respect of the items not affected by the break in the chain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the break in itself may not have affected the outcome given the High Court's reasoning.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, there can be no excuse for this lapse on the part of the Police officer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a breach of a legal requirement; it is also a breach of Police protocol, both of which require the Police to respond to a crime scene promptly, or as soon as practicable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The broader objective of these requirements is to ensure the integrity of relevant evidence by securing it into Police custody or otherwise obtaining a proper record of it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether there has to be a seizure in any specific case must depend on the facts of the case, the nature of the exhibits and evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, even if there is no seizure, it is necessary to obtain a proper record of the evidence, such as by careful photography of the items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, careful photography, soon after the Police report was filed, may have been good enough.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have nevertheless asked for an explanation as to why this has happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am told that the officer involved had a number of other on-going cases, prosecutions, arrest operations and a very personal matter that he had to deal with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He seems to have been under a lot of pressure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a situation that many Home Team officers find themselves in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a reality of what our officers go through.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I must say, Sir, I have noticed in various parts of the Civil Service, quite a lot of our officers are under work pressure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have mentioned it at other points in this House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Technology has helped, will help, but that has limits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point that the High Court made about the Police was that "poor quality" black-and-white photos were shown to Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police agree that colour photos would have been more effective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police's review has shown that the layout of the photographs was also not satisfactory.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some photos featured multiple items in a single photograph, with some overlapping and partially obscured.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third point the High Court made: the inaccuracies in recording the statements, the pace at which the questions were asked and the time when one statement was taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And thirdly, the provision of a Bahasa Indonesia interpreter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have dealt with the interpretation issue earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On this issue, I have said to Police officers we need to make sure accused persons understand the statement recording process, what it involves, what is required of them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have asked the Police to ask what language the person wishes to speak, which they do, but also explain briefly what the process entails and the purpose of the statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that the accused may ask for an interpreter at any time and that this should be recorded as part of the statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court also pointed out that there were inaccuracies in the way questions were phrased and there were grammatical errors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police have said to me that it is difficult to make sure there are no grammatical errors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think everybody agrees they need to try and make sure grammatical errors, if any, should not affect the interpretation and understanding of the statement itself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, the timing is inevitable, because of the legal requirement to release a person under investigation, within 48 hours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police will have to make an assessment on whether the person is capable of understanding the questions at the time the statements are taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said, Police will take the comments on board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court also made observations about the AGC on how the functionality of the DVD player was demonstrated in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC has filed an affidavit explaining its position on record.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The matter is now the subject of disciplinary proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And thus, I will refrain from commenting on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have been given a detailed note by AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can set out the position, but I prefer not to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be full account of what the DPPs did, at the Disciplinary Tribunal or DT.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The key question before us is whether there was any improper influence on them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Indranee has discussed this with Mr Pritam Singh, the Leader of the Opposition, who was also concerned that we should not go into this in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think lawyers will understand why we take this approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC has also identified specific areas where it needs to improve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the valuation of items that are the subject of property offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, the valuation of the items in the charges were derived from the Liew family's estimates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This has been the general practice hitherto, to rely on the complainant's assessment of the value.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are currently no formal guidelines for Prosecutors on the issue of valuation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prosecutors are expected to use their judgement and discretion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Independent assessment of the value of the items may have helped in respect of some of the items in this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, AGC is also looking at how it prepares for trials and will seek to learn from this and other cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a further, but general and important point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prosecution's overarching role is to ensure that justice is done and not to win the case at all costs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point is not being made by reference to this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC has consistently emphasised this point to all its officers and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Attorney-General himself has also publicly stressed his Chambers' commitment to the principle of even-handed justice, in his speeches at the Openings of the Legal Year, and elsewhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, I will move to the High Court's views on the State Court's judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, some background on cases dealt with by the State Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Courts deal with most of the criminal cases in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: About 10% of these appeals succeed, for instance, in setting aside the convictions or reducing the sentence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This 10% of cases – there can be different views on evidence, on law, the exigencies of trial process, for example, witnesses say different things or something new turns up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court disagreed with the Trial Judge's assessment of the evidence and made observations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With that as background, I will say the views expressed by the High Court fall within the range of cases where an Appellate Court disagrees with a Lower Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some of these cases, the Appellate Court does take a different interpretation of the evidence, draws different inferences, comes to different conclusions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the function of the Appellate Court when it takes the view that the Lower Court has made an error.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, even between the High Court and Court of Appeal, there are differences of view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, in one of the cases Mohamed Affandi bin Rosli v PP & anor   1 SLR 440, chain of custody issues also arose.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question for us, as I have said more than once, is not which Court was right or wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The key question: was the case conducted fairly in both Courts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Court heard evidence from 12 Prosecution witnesses, four Defence witnesses, including Ms Liyani, over 20 days.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It had the opportunity to observe the witnesses, consider their evidence, Ms Liyani’s submissions, and it made its findings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court considered the Lower Court’s findings and Ms Liyani’s further submissions over three days and came to a different view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This became a long and somewhat complex, or complicated, case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Record of Proceedings runs to almost 3,700 pages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have brought this House through some of the issues in detail, as I said earlier, to give Members a slightly better appreciation of the evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The matter was thoroughly ventilated and considered by both the State Courts and the High Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was one of those 10% of cases where the Appeal Court disagreed with the Lower Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are questions about some aspects of one or more of the Liews’ evidence and conduct, the claim of ownership of some items and the valuation by them – that appears to have been quite cavalier, to say the least.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Questions also arise about Ms Liyani’s conduct and evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court gave Ms Liyani the benefit of doubt because it was troubled by one or more of the Liews’ evidence and conduct, and because there were questions relating to her statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are aspects of trial preparation where Police and AGC can improve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have gone through all of this because we have to show the Police and the AGC did not act arbitrarily, or as the result of the influence of a rich and influential family.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those were the accusations that circulated immediately after the learned Justice Chan issued his judgment – that there was a grave miscarriage of justice, and AGC and the Police were asked to apologise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I put forward to this House show that the Police and AGC had good grounds to charge Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They certainly did not act at the behest of the Liew family.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this is how our system is supposed to work – Police and AGC made up their assessments based on the evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Court agreed with the prosecution and convicted Ms Liyani.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court disagreed, overtuned the conviction, felt there were reasonable grounds to doubt the motives of the Liew family in making the Police report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rest, Sir, I will deal with in Part 2.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I have said is the fundamental question relating to our systems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I wonder, Sir, if this is an appropriate time to take a break.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I propose to take a break now and take the Sitting at 4.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.50 pm until 4.10 pm.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here, I want to go into the broader questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The key question is whether the case was handled differently because of the status of the complainant or if there has been any improper influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Really, if I were to put it this way – did LML in any way influence these proceedings or was the case investigated and prosecuted in accordance with the rules like any other case?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have set out how the Police handled the matter and what they took into account.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Decisions were taken by them, together with their immediate supervisor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one senior has spoken with or been influenced by LML or any of the Liews on this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meaning, as I said, it was dealt with by the IOs and their immediate supervisor and no one beyond that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Turning to AGC, I have explained how the matter was dealt with by AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was dealt with by DPPs and cleared at the level of a Director.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, neither LML nor anyone acting for them, approached AGC or had any contact with AGC in this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been some questions asked specific to the Attorney-General, that he was on the Board of Directors of Capitaland between 20 November 2000 and 2 January 2006 when LML was the President and CEO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As a result, did AG in any way influence the proceedings?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AG resigned from the Capitaland Board with effect from 2 January 2006.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He resigned because he had a difference of viewpoints with LML on some issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When AGC conducted its internal review on this matter, AG recused himself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, AG had nothing to do with this case at any stage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The case was conducted by the State Courts in open Court in accordance with the Rules.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This case is, in fact, an illustration of how the Rule of Law applies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A foreign domestic worker is charged, the High Court acquits her, the Complainant is a wealthy, powerful person, but all are equal before the Law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not matter who the parties are, Justice according to the facts and the Law as the Courts see it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We may agree or disagree with the State Court's or High Court’s decisions and conclusions, but that is a different matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at it at a systemic level, at the highest level, you talk about the criminal justice system – we have the Police who investigate in accordance with the legal framework for Police investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC make the charging decision based on available evidence and public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Trial Courts consider the sufficiency of the evidence and the legal issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Appellate Courts review the decision of the Trial Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The case shows that the criminal justice system, as a whole, works.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you drill down to the next level, we have "systems".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, these would comprise investigative protocols, SOPs for how the Police and the DPPs operate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have mentioned some errors that were made, we have to try and strengthen the "systems" at that level, try and prevent re-occurrence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Besides these levels to the system, there will always be the risk of mistakes by individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These lapses will have to be dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is even more important in the current zeitgeist that is sweeping through countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Societies around the world are grappling with debates on inequality, a sense that the elite are creaming off most of the economic benefits and bending the rules and systems to their advantage, and in the process buying off, suborning those in Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People are fed up with unfair structures; equal opportunities are drying up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, we are not in the same situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our active intervention in socio-economic issues has helped most people to benefit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But our people know we must jealously guard the availability of equal opportunities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must ensure that everyone has a fair shake.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must be alert, guard against the wealthy and the powerful taking unfair advantages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a significant section of our people feel that the system favours some, or that it is unfairly stacked against them, then Singapore will lose its cohesion and it cannot succeed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, it is essential that we have a fair system, that we have a clean system, that we have a system that gives opportunities to all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If LML did unfairly influence the proceedings, then it will be a hit to our foundations and it will be a hit to our sense of fairness, equality and justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And a dent to Project Singapore itself because Singapore is built on these ideals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have always been jealous about guarding against such corrosion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not mean that there will be no abuse of power and no corruption.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when it happens, swift, decisive action must be taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will know successive Governments have been clear about this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There has to be a ruthless intensity in upholding integrity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was one of the most senior Members in Mr Lee Kuan Yew’s Cabinet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when corruption allegations surfaced, Mr Lee directed the CPIB to conduct investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee said at that time, and I quote, "There is no way a Minister can avoid investigations and a trial if there is evidence to support one." These were the values of our Founding Generation and these are and have to be our continuing values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have been scrupulously stressed and adhered to by the two succeeding Prime Ministers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When there is a breach, action is taken, will be taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2012, you had Mr Howard Shaw, then-Executive Director of the Singapore Environment Council, convicted for obtaining commercial sex with minors; had asked for a nominal fine based on testimonials of his good character and social standing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Court found no exceptional circumstances; 12 weeks' imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sentence was to provide a strong deterrent to others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Peter Lim was a senior Home Team officer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In many countries, his actions would not have attracted criminal punishment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In most countries, Commissioners of SCDF, Assistant Directors of CPIB, are pretty much untouchable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is not only corruption that we must guard against.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must also guard against what I call soft corruption and influence peddling.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1984, Mr Lee said, and I quote, "We exercised power as trustees for the people, with an abiding sense of our fiduciary responsibility.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our honour, our sense of duty made us exercise power scrupulously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have curbed, restrained, prevented any distortion of policies which would have been inevitable if the personal interests of the few in charge were allowed full rein.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the case in many new countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When those in office regard the power vested in them as a personal prerogative, they inevitably enrich themselves, promote their families, favour their friends.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fundamental structures of the modern state are eroded, like the supporting beams of a house after termites have attacked them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, the people have to pay dearly and long for the sins and crimes of their leaders.” And as early as 1961, the late Dr Goh warned about the risks, that groups of elites might create an environment that would favour one community at the expense of another.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In an article in Nanyang University journal, 1961, he said, and I quote, "To achieve an honest and energetic administration appears easy in theory.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In practice, very few of the young and emergent nations have achieved this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even in the most advanced and leading societies, whether communist or democratic, the problem of nepotism is a recurring one and can only be countered by constant vigilance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In advanced societies, it is not so much open nepotism that is to be feared, but the insidious 'old boy' type whereby no illegalities are committed, but in which the pinnacles of power, influence and wealth are the reserve of those born into the right families.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In underdeveloped countries, the matter could be more serious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A system may arise in which the dominant majority, whether of families, clans or even entire communities, arrogates to itself not only the openings to the seats of power, but also the avenues by which individuals can fit themselves out for such positions of power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The dominant majority is thus able to point out that those outside of the charmed circle just do not have the necessary qualifications to be admitted to this elite group.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, many able and aspiring people are denied the opportunity for the full use of their abilities." I personally find these words very powerful, insightful and have more than once quoted this speech of Dr Goh in my own speeches because Dr Goh, I think, has identified precisely a serious, insidious risk in any society including ours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are not that special that we can be immune to these risks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to constantly make sure that we do not allow it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to be very careful to try and stamp it out wherever it appears, and make no mistake, make no mistake.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will keep appearing in big and small ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is again something successive Prime Ministers have been vigilant about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One illustration of that is the letter that the Prime Minister sends out at the start of each new term of the House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will quote parts: "the context each time may be different but the subject remains constant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must never tire of reminding ourselves of their importance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One vital factor to retain the trust of Singaporeans all these years is honesty and integrity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A few will cultivate you to obtain benefits for themselves or their companies, to gain respectability by association with you, or to get you to influence Ministries and Statutory Boards, to make decisions in their favour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Personal favours, big and small, are just some of the countless social lubricants which such people use to ingratiate themselves to MPs and make you obliged to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At all times, be seen to be beyond the influence of gifts or favours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Separate your public political position from your private, professional or business interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MPs who are in business, who occupy senior management positions in companies or who sit on company boards, should be especially vigilant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have held our position because our integrity has never been in doubt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Always conduct yourselves with modesty, decorum, dignity." I can tell Members this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is all not just nice sounding advice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even before it reaches the kind of conduct referred to in the Prime Minister’s letter, if we feel that there is some conduct that requires a closer look, we do take a closer look.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am referring here to conduct which is not criminal, not a breach of ethics, but which in our view should be avoided; something that may be legal but, for example, lead eventually to something which is not of so good odour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we sense that, I usually have a chat with the relevant MP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They come, have a cup of coffee with me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But do not worry, it does not happen every time people come and have coffee with me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it is criminal, of course, there will be prosecution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there have been MPs and ex-MPs who have been prosecuted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
