text: If there are breaches of other rules, the respective professional or regulatory bodies will take action, as they have done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not intervene or try and stop any of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have dealt with this at some length because we must understand these are fundamental values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if we do not keep them, we will be in trouble.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, in this context, we have a more challenging environment because we are a small place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A lot of people know each other – many educational, professional, work-related, social familial connections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Same schools, colleges, Universities, time spent in National Service, other connections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We try and look for the people on the basis of merit and they will often, because of their careers and education, have deep connection with many others whom they interact with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The way we handle this – make sure the persons appointed are men and women of character.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have the moral fibre to do the right thing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What will the position be if he was, in fact, a close friend of LML?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will expect him to disclose that and recuse himself as well from any decision making.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prof S Jayakumar, when he was Minister for Law, what were his connections?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When he was Dean, Law School, the then-AG’s wife had been his Vice-Dean.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong had been his law school contemporary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Former Commissioner of Police Goh Yong Hong was also his law school contemporary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the succeeding Commissioner of Police Tee Tua Ba was Prof Jaya’s law student.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Attorney-General and I were his law students as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had spent 22 years in private practice; I worked with many Senior Counsels, senior lawyers, appeared before many Judges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our small size means these connections and interactions are inevitable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And so, we will always have to be very careful, always remember we are fiduciaries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do not allow any corrosion of public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Be worthy of the trust people have reposed in us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is critical that, whatever the relationship, the Government maintains high standards of probity, of conduct so that decisions are made on objective and impartial assessment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And have we lived up to those standards?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We rank highly on credible international indices, for absence of corruption, for rule of law, for the way our system functions cleanly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a country known for all these – and that continues to be the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What happens if you allow the system to go awry?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What happens when you allow corruption, abuse of position, abuse of power?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Influence peddling has become part and parcel of politics and governance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The US Supreme Court has said: “Ingratiation and access embody a central feature of democracy.” Not against the law for officials to set up meetings, host events, call other officials on behalf of lobbyists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I personally think this is not good for the healthy functioning of society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Lobbying itself in the US is a massive business.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The experience of South Africa offers another example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In South Africa, "State Capture" is a buzzword because of how private interests have exerted influence over government decision-making and used this influence to plunder the state.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Corruption scandals involving the former President and the Gupta brothers are the most famous examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is, of course, an extreme example of the system going awry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The critical question for us: how do we ensure that the system stays clean, that we do not allow what Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Dr Goh Keng Swee warned against?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have a media that highlights these issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: See the number of articles that have appeared on this matter in the Singapore media - accountability, because a well-educated, aware population that holds us accountable; and Parliament, where we have these issues to be openly discussed, debated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the top is clean, then your systems can work well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have got to make sure of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if it starts, then very few things can save such a country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, if we had seen anything wrong by way of influence peddling, swift, open, transparent action would have been taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now I will deal with the questions Members have raised by way of Parliamentary Questions, or PQs, which I have not already dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Derrick Goh have asked a number of questions about the High Court’s observations, the agencies’ processes, the internal reviews and related questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Part 1 of my Statement has covered these points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Mr Derrick Goh have also asked for some information on foreign domestic workers, theft cases, Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said earlier, Police investigate around 14,000, in fact, 14,122 theft-related cases – I think that was in 2016.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On average, about 70, or 27% of the 255 foreign domestic workers, were prosecuted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not track data on how many of them claimed trial or how many of them had legal representation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This includes cases of physical and sexual abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if foreign domestic workers and other work permit holders can be accompanied by non-legal personnel, similar to the Appropriate Adults, or AAs, scheme, for Police interviews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From 2015 to 2019, an average of 2,741 foreign workers on work permits were arrested each year as potential accused.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have earlier said Police are already very stretched.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Appropriate Adults attended to 2,300 activations in 2019.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These cases involved minors and mentally vulnerable persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we had to provide AAs for every foreign worker interviewed, we would have to minimally double the current volunteer pool, provide the training and resourcing; and some may require more than one statement, and this will become a real constraint and load on the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And each time you have an interview, you have to look for an Appropriate Adult.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Interviews will be delayed if the AA is not available.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The key is for Police to make sure that the foreign workers understand the questions and their answers are properly recorded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it has to be open for scrutiny in Court, which it is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So that Members can understand the load on our officers, I will share the following.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, Police investigated 66,200 criminal cases in 2016 and they were handled by 1,100 IOs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we were to have the same numbers as Hong Kong, we would need 9,100 more officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My entire Police force today comprises 13,200 Police officers, including National Servicemen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we were to have the same numbers as Hong Kong, we would have to have 9,000 more officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we were to have the same numbers as London, we would need 6,000 more officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we were to have the same numbers as New York, we would need 11,000 more officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Members can understand and appreciate the load on our officers and, as I have said, I have spoken about this in the House more than once.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And my concern is that there is a limit to how much our officers can do with increasing workload and increasing expectations, but without a proportionate increase in manpower.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked how many State Court Judges had previously worked as prosecutors in the AGC and whether the Ministry will review the policy of separation of duties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This point has come up previously and let me put it this way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The total number of lawyers in our Legal Service and Judiciary, excluding High Court Judges, is 801.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this context, the question is: why are officers posted between the State Courts and other parts of the Legal Service?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can there be independence if they are liable to be cross-posted?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr A P Rajah, a former Speaker and High Court Judge, said in 1963: “He thinks that if you are a DPP, then you cannot be a good District Judge; if you are a District Judge, then you cannot be a good DPP; if you are a first-rate DPP, then you cannot make a first-rate Assize Judge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Merely to say that because one has been a DPP and that, therefore, when he gets on to the Bench, he is going to side with the prosecution, is not correct and is not fair to the profession.” I am not suggesting that Mr Lim Biow Chuan or anyone else is under any misapprehension.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this was said in 1963 when the number of officers was much smaller.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, all movements in the Legal Service are overseen by Personnel Boards and/or Committees all chaired by the Chief Justice, and the Legal Service Commission, of which the Chief Justice is the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Legal Service Commission takes the view that rotation has three major benefits.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, it provides access to a larger pool of talent to select State Court Judges with the right blend of temperament, knowledge and experience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two, it develops Legal Service Officers (LSOs) into well-rounded officers by exposing them to, and training them in, different fields of legal work and allowing them to learn about their strengths and weaknesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this benefits the Legal Service and Singapore, no matter where the LSOs are posted in future.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three, this also gives flexibility, for instance, to accommodate LSOs who want to try different types of work, or LSOs who have a change of heart about their preferred line of work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Judges who have prosecutorial experience will bring added knowledge to the work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: LSOs on the Judicial track are posted to jobs within the Judicial Branch and they are assessed by a separate Judicial Branch Special Personnel Board headed by the Chief Justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister explained why this was done: “We need a first-class Legal Service that in turn calls for a first-class personnel management system to attract and retain the best people, to remunerate them fairly with reference to the market, to groom talent systematically and prepare them for leadership positions and to imbue officers with the right values and commitment to Singapore." Up to now, we have always decided to stick to the integrated model because we had too few officers to support two separate services and we believed that LSOs would have a better career path in one single integrated service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is timely for us to review the position again, in the light of changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, because the Legal Service is much larger, so officers can specialise without conscribing their career prospects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, because the scope and complexity of work, whether in the Government Ministries, whether in AGC or in the Courts, the scope of work has in all cases grown enormously in the Government, in the Ministries – there are more responsibilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Eligible officers can elect to specialise along either track.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will then be posted to jobs within either the Legal Branch or the Judicial Branch.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These Boards manage the LSOs in the respective Branches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, even as we promote more specialisation, it is critical that the Legal Service operates as an integrated whole.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The specialisation into the two tracks is for the middle ranks of the Legal Service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Junior officers starting out on their careers will still be posted to different departments and across branches to develop them in different fields of legal work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond Grade 3, the senior officers at Grade 2 and above will still be managed by the Legal Service Commission because at that level of seniority, there will only be very few officers and it is necessary to continue with the integrated model to provide better career options and flexibility in deployment to meet the needs of the Service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The approach we have adopted strikes a balance between specialisation and integration, with safeguards for judicial independence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we think that this is what is good for Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai has asked whether there can be an expedited trial process for foreign economically vulnerable accused persons and he has also asked about the interpretation services in SPF.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Depends on the nature of the case, availability of counsels, DPPs, how long the trial itself takes, documents, witnesses, challenges that the Prosecution and Defence make, and time taken for deliberation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The State Courts, as I said earlier, handle about 600 criminal trials per year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have 55 judges to handle these trials.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, it is a very heavy load for the State Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we expedite a case for a foreign person, then a Singaporean accused will have to wait even longer, if we take Mr Leong Mun Wai's suggestion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He claimed trial to the charges against him and was remanded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the Public Prosecutor's request, the trial was brought forward and conducted on an urgent basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be many other cases like this but even if there is no specific remand situation, if you bring forward some people in the queue, the others in the queue will have to wait longer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not think it is fair to Singaporeans to do what Mr Leong Mun Wai has suggested.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, on the interpretation service, I have given a fairly extensive answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police currently employ a pool of interpreters for the three official working languages – that is, Chinese, Malay and Tamil – as well as more common local dialects – Hokkien, Teochew and Cantonese.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police will engage the services of interpreters if the interviewee is unable to understand the language used by the interviewer or vice versa.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For foreign languages, the Police will engage the services of foreign language interpreters on an ad hoc basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a framework to assess the suitability of interpreters, which includes their qualifications and relevant work experience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regards Ms Liyani in this case, she was asked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point is: does the interviewee understand the language being used?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as I said earlier, the Police have been told – they must really check this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain and Mr Leong Mun Wai have asked about increasing legal aid for accused in criminal cases; and secondly, increasing the honoraria paid for lawyers under CLAS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Carrie Tan has specifically also asked if we will consider having a public defender scheme to defend accused persons in criminal cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: CLAS aims to provide legal aid to persons facing non-capital charges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is administered by the Law Society's Pro Bono Services, or LSPBS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The initiative came from the Law Society, senior lawyers, in particular the late Mr Harry Elias.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it was an outstanding initiative by the profession.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is in place a framework, an assessment process, means and merit tests applied in each case to try and ensure that funding is targeted, allocated to applicants who are most vulnerable and who genuinely need assistance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This goes towards general operating costs, including staff salaries and overheads.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I announced it and it started from 2015.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: CLAS funds the remaining 25% of its costs through private donations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this sum is also used to defend foreigners who need criminal legal aid.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The honoraria that is paid is extremely nominal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a system where the Government funds some part; the private sector funds some part, through cash donations, lawyers giving their time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Should we change the model and go for full Government-funded criminal legal aid?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will just give the experience of two countries though we can look at many countries' experiences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The United Kingdom, or at least England and Wales, offer a fully government-funded criminal legal aid scheme which comprises both a public defender scheme with in-house government lawyers and a legal aid scheme that outsources cases to private lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There has been much public debate and outcry in the UK over these schemes for various reasons, including abuse and escalating government costs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, there has been much unhappiness over the large legal aid fees, especially evident in cases where legal aid was spent on lengthy trials for defendants who were ultimately convicted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, three men who were accused of the murder of a policeman known as Andrew Harper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When they tried to evade arrest, he tried arresting them, they killed him, it cost the UK taxpayer S$817,000 in legal aid fees in 2008.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they were convicted of manslaughter in the end.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another case was that of Ben Butler and his partner Jennie Gray, who were convicted of murdering Butler's six-year-old daughter and of child cruelty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Both were granted nearly S$2.64 million in legal aid expenses, covering both their criminal cases and a custody battle with the child's grandparents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been many reports about rich defendants who received legal aid as their assets were frozen, but they remained wealthy enough as the state did not manage to seize all their assets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Around 50 defendants with more than S$1.76 million in illegally obtained assets were found to have received legal aid in 2012.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These defendants were ordered to repay their legal aid costs but some failed to pay up despite court demands.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given the large legal aid costs, it has been difficult for the UK government to sustain this level of spending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The government has had to implement drastic cuts to legal aid budgets since 2012, but these reforms were strongly opposed by the legal industry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Lawyers deemed the reformed fee schedules to be inadequate, went on strikes in 2014 and again, in 2018, to oppose cuts, disrupting court proceedings and delaying the resolution of criminal cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You must note: once you make legal aid a requirement, then you cannot proceed with the case until you find a lawyer who is willing to handle it for the fees that he proposes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we take Ms Liyani's case as an example, the Defence Counsel has estimated that if full fees were charged, it could have cost about $150,000.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we make criminal legal aid a requirement, then the taxpayers will have to pay that amount or whatever the Defence Counsel requires.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could be more, it could be less, or have the trial postponed until a lawyer is found.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I welcome suggestions but Members, please look at these points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, when you make your points, maybe offer concrete suggestions on how we can avoid what has happened elsewhere, if we want to go down this route.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hong Kong has a fully government-funded public defender scheme that outsources part of its cases to private lawyers and the Law Society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is why we have been very careful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also looked at the situation in Australia, New Zealand – raised similar issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would go into them, but we knew it can get very costly and very difficult to manage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in our situation, we have actually been very fortunate because our legal profession has worked with Law Society, the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has been a cooperative relationship and a strong public spirit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It means our lawyers do well in the other areas and we are able to encourage the pro bono spirit at the same time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai has asked can we increase the honoraria that is paid to lawyers under CLAS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My preference is to keep the probono spirit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A mix of lawyers employed specifically by CLAS, small number; lawyers from private sector, coming in – I think it is a better approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, our approach has been legal aid for those who truly need it with public and private partnership, tapping on the excellent pro bono spirit of our lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are also not completely satisfied with the current model.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How can we better help those who cannot pay for lawyers and yet, make sure that we do not go down the road that other countries have travelled?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, we reached the five-year mark since the enhanced CLAS was announced in 2014.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, CLAS was originally initiated in 1985 by the late Mr Harry Elias, together with a group of lawyers, to better help those who could not pay for a lawyer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2015, pursuant to my announcement in 2014, we enhanced CLAS, with the support of the legal profession and we started reviewing the enhanced model last year which is the five-year mark since we made the first announcement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been considering different possibilities, including possibly a public defender's office.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should also mention that in 2014, when we announced the enhanced CLAS, some in the legal profession were very concerned that this was going to eat into their rice bowl.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We received a petition from some lawyers – not that few – about the possible adverse effect of the enhanced CLAS on their work, on their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah and I met some of these concerned members from the criminal bar in 2014.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We showed them the figures – that we were not going to take away their work, that we were helping those who could not have gone to them anyway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People need to be helped and that is central to the Government's mission.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our profession has 781 firms who have between one and five lawyers in the firm.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of these 781, 233 firms practise criminal law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In terms of lawyers, there are about 750 lawyers who practise criminal law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many depend heavily on the smaller value legal work on criminal cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We should aim to have a structure that helps those who truly need help but does not become an unacceptable strain on the treasury.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For those who can afford to pay for lawyers, the taxpayer should not have to pay for them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Law Society is in principle supportive of expanding criminal legal aid in order to enhance access to justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, the Law Society's council has expressed strong concerns on the impact on paid work, especially for small firms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They had doubts as to whether this proposed expansion that the Government has been discussing with them would so neatly capture Singaporeans who could not afford lawyers' fees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The criminal bar representatives have counter-proposed to expand the coverage of offences, rather than increase the means test coverage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have used the term "public defender's office" assuming that everyone understands what it means.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Maybe I should explain. "Public defender's office" means the Government pays for the lawyers, employs the lawyers in a separate structure, and they act in criminal cases to defend the accused; with a suitable means test and a suitable merits test. "How many officers?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How much?" are conversations we have to have with MOF, amongst others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in principle, we will have to first discuss it with the profession and then talk to MOF and deal with the issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in principle, our approach, I think, might have to go down that route and at least my Ministry, MinLaw, is in favour of this approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai has asked for a Committee of Inquiry to consider the conduct of the Police and AGC in relation to Ms Liyani's case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now that I have shown the Member this, I think he will acknowledge his request is legally not doable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Member really wants another inquiry into this matter, then what will be necessary is a Commission of Inquiry, not a Committee of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Liyani's case was dealt with as a routine case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have set out the facts, what has happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It shows clearly there was a good prima facie case to proceed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is also the Disciplinary Tribunal which will inquire into the complaint against the AGC officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thus, before we have a Commission of Inquiry, which is a serious matter, will take up resources, lots of time, more and more work, the Member should specify what part of this matter continues to reasonably make him believe and question that undue influence was used, by the Liews?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What exactly by reference to what the Police did and what AGC did?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would like him to tell us, Sir, before I carry on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason I raised a question is to try to first establish a principle.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, the Minister had provided a lot more information today, which I fully appreciate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I did not have those information when I raised this question and proposition but still, after listening to the Minister, I think that there is still a need to have an independent inquiry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As to what form it takes, I think the Minister has explained.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Maybe we have to go to the level of the Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think Singaporeans are expecting that we do further investigation into this case, not just about the influence peddling but also about the systemic aspect of the whole criminal justice system, that maybe we need to look at various aspects which, actually, the Minister has enlightened us tremendously today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the evidence gathering, contamination and when the Court refers to – I am not a lawyer, no legal training but I was told by lawyers it could be called evidence contamination and all those things.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And also, about how AGC had made the decision and about whether there is a need to have a public defender's office and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All these things, I thought, are very enlightening, but I think it requires more discussion so that we can come up with a better system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not make any sense, but let us move on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All I want to know, the public defender's office, for example, the Commission of Inquiry will have nothing to do with that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Mr Leong, can I ask you, a Commission of Inquiry is a serious business.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as I said, it is not a question of making some broad and vague statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not a question of saying, "I am not a lawyer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have set out in the House what has happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would expect you to be able to tell me based on what you have heard which part leaves you concerned with either the influence peddling issue or any other issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mean, waht do we have a Commission of Inquiry on the entire legal, the Police and enforcement system?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, can we please have some clarity on what is it that concerns you?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume you have read the key material.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume you knew that there was something specific or a set of specific issues that you want to focus on – which is why you asked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is it that you want the Commission of Inquiry to look into which has gone wrong?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have told you what happened with the translation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it the fact that they took five weeks – the Police – to go and look for the items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have told you what has happened and I told you there are disciplinary proceedings against the officer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, Minister, I think one issue, for example, after listening to your Statement, specifically, I was thinking, for example, you mentioned about the Police having taken five weeks to attend to the evidence.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You said that there were some lapses but nevertheless, the manpower situation is very tight.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, to me, even if the manpower situation is tight, do they need five weeks to attend to the evidence, for example.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am quoting this as an example, because I think there are many aspects as I said just now that need further investigation so that we can come up with whole integrated and overall look at the whole systemic aspect of of the criminal justice process, so that we can come up with a better solution.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is the reason why I have recommended that we have an independent inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said there is no excuse but I asked for an explanation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police do not in any way seek to defend it, but we gave an explanation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said there are manpower issues but that is not an excuse and the officer is facing disciplinary proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what is it about the five weeks that concerns you?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He should not have taken that length of time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: His reasonings will be gone into and he will be dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is there any other issue that you are concerned about?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If that is the case for the five weeks, then we will take it as that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For another aspect, for example, you have been trying to interpret LML's behaviour and his family's behaviour.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Their interpretation could also be further, sort of, investigated and analysed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For example, in terms of the misbehaviour, it is quite common that when we have the maid at home, we do actually have some leeway for her to do certain things, to the extent that sometimes she takes something and you know —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, we can call an inquiry into any issue.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, you have been asked, what specific issues do you have that warrants asking for this Commission?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How they interact with each other cannot be the subject of a Government Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained why it is not to cast doubt on anything but to say we had to investigate because the High Court made some observations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now I have the information in my hand, I have no choice but in duty of frankness, I have got to put it to this House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is not the business of the Commissions of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: At the same time, you have an interpretation of the motive and you have the benefit of having new information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The interpretation of motive has got nothing to do with the Government, Government organs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have just explained why that was put forward.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got nothing to do with how the Police proceeded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got nothing to do with how AGC proceeded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is something that has come out in the course of the investigations, subsequent investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How is that a subject matter of a Commission of Inquiry?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, but then when there is new information, coupled with the information that came out of the Court process, do we not have to get to the bottom of it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This House is now dealing with whether there was any improper influence exerted on AGC or the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have given you categorical confirmations as to at which level this was handled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It cannot properly be the object of a Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, Minister, I think what I am trying to drive at is that the whole case probably requires more investigation and interpretation of the facts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, if you think that is enough then I will withdraw my proposition or recommendation for an independent inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have to say, Mr Leong, it is not right to come here and say, "I think that a Commission of Inquiry is necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I cannot tell you what my concerns are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in general, you know, it is good to have a Commission of Inquiry." Commissions of Inquiry do not proceed that way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have no problem recommending such a Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Obviously, I am not saying this without having consulted with my Cabinet colleagues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Cabinet will be prepared to recommend a Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have nothing to hide, completely transparent about this issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is not, in law, they would say, micawberism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not because something strikes your mind and suddenly you get this idea, that we have Commissions of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have had several weeks now since the High Court judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh wants to raise a point.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Would you like to raise a point, Mr Pritam Singh?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I thought you wanted to take part in the exchange.

speaker: Mr Pritam
text: I want to pursue a different line of inquiry!

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am always happy to hear from you, Mr Singh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But so far we have heard nothing that I can rationally put together to justify a Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I have answered all the Members' questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if Mr Singh wants to ask something, so yes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: One pertains to the comments made by Minister on the lapse vis-a-vis investigations from the 30 October to 3 December.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This was in Part 1 of Minister's Statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think from the public perspective, there is a concern when investigations for whatever purposes are somewhat not conducted properly or what the Minister said, "in breach of Police's requirements".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, my question really is what is the extent of this issue?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the concern is, moving forward, how significant does the Minister assess this matter to be?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can it be a matter that can be resolved by directives or circulars from the Commanding Officers of various Divisions?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second is pertaining to a statement that I believe that was made today by the NGO HOME about a complaint that Ms Parti Liyani lodged against the Police concerning the way the IO conducted himself at trial.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My last issue – actually, it is not a question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister spoke earlier of sharing some Annexes with Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If I heard him right, he said the Annexes would be outside the Chamber.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not believe there are any Annexes outside.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Are those other Annexes going to be shared now or will we receive them later?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That is just a question of order, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the Annexes, Mr Singh, there was a set that they were distributing but let me go and check.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think other Members also say they do not have it, so I will check.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, it is not to be treated as a precedent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The broader reason for this is, of course, a matter of concern.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I have given you the broader statistics and you can understand in every aspect of policing work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not a matter unknown to you all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Ms Sylvia Lim has raised it more than once in this House about the pressure that lack of manpower resources have put the Police under.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the statement by HOME, I have not been able to look at it very carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we have focused, in my Ministerial Statement, on what the Judge dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As far as I am concerned, those are the issues that are raised, that I have to deal with here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is a specific concern about what has been set out in the HOME statement, a question can be put up and we can deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Though it arises from a Police report that Ms Liyani has made – not Ms Liyani, I think HOME had made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One was the translation issue that I had dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other was the fact that five weeks were taken, which I have dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I really wonder how these are matters for filing of a Police report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fact that the IO took five weeks is a matter that a victim files a Police report to complain about?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am not suggesting that anybody in this House is responsible for it.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Minister has spoken about the issue of motive by the Liews.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, we got information which we had to set out to this House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That information was not before the High Court, as I said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said that the High Court ruled the inference that it did, naturally and understandably, based on the information that it had.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am not in a position to say anything really beyond that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is in relation to the duration of the case – four years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Four years is a fairly long time for a person not to be employed, and then, eventually, acquitted.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, would he be able to explain the four-year duration?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second point is about entrenchment of impartiality within the system, what more can be done to entrench impartiality.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am not insinuating that it does not exist.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But what can we do more to entrench it?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It relates to capital cases – whether in capital cases, in trials, there can be two judges hearing a capital case in the first instance, and then possibly five judges on appeal, arising from the various different opinions between each levels of court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It took about six months because of the number of items and the Police had to check the items and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the first pre-trial conference was in late 2017, if I am not wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the case was then tried in 2018.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The High Court hearing took place in 2019 on appeal and judgment was delivered in 2020.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the High Court hearing took place over three different tranches and spread over from 2019 to early 2020.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it was a question of dates as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, these are matters that are not really within our control.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr de Souza had another question on entrenchment of impartiality; what more we can do?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to take very seriously what I said just now, about we got to be always on guard to see some sort of — Explicit bias, we can all see.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But implicit bias, growing in, we have got to guard against that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the system we have today is the best that we can find in the sense that the Police have a clear role.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not insignificant, but at the same time it is not as if every case goes for prosecution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is what I meant by the system at the top level.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police, AGC, State Courts, High Court – all working independently as they should; looking at it, and hopefully the right result is arrived at.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Good people across all the different parts, clear rules, transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When people ask questions, we have to be accountable here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if something goes wrong, the will to put it right as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think those are the things that you need to look at and to be very alert about any kind of influence peddling.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question on capital cases, this is something that has been discussed previously – whether we ought to have two judges instead of one.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had two judges and then we moved to one judge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know that you need five judges on appeal, necessarily.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this is something that we will discuss with the Courts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I just have a clarification in regard to confusion or the alleged confusion on the statements.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are there any plans to video record all statements taken from accused persons?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Actually, if you could do video recording, that is a gold standard.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One way is to say we just take a video and use that as evidence, but it could be a three-hour session, or four-hour session.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It means AGC will have to spend three hours trying to look at it and then, re-look at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As opposed to reading a transcript, which is much faster, and time wise, it does not work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise, in the Courts, both at pretrial conferences as well as hearings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And internally, the Police – both have an infrastructure issue in terms of the kind of rooms that are needed, equipped for this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is something we can overcome with a lot of money and further resources.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the manpower needed to transcribe is very difficult in this case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have been bottlenecked on moving on to a wider and wider range of cases for video recording because of the administrative processes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we have tried outside providers, that has not worked well either, because we saw a lot of errors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you know, in statement-taking, when you see from Ms Liyani's case, statement-taking can be can be a serious issue in court, with what the words mean or what the words are said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, when we have used outside providers that has resulted in problems too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have had to sit back and redo all the statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: While I would like to go down this route, we have had some difficulties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another issue that arises I think in relation to vulnerable victims is whether or not they should have earlier access to legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, accused are allowed to access to legal counsel after a reasonable time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In other systems, it is allowed at an earlier time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I would the Minister consider earlier access to legal counsel?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Vikram Nair is a lawyer, he knows that access is allowed within a reasonable time after investigations begin.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It seeks to strike a balance between the rights of the accused and public interest, to ensure thorough, objective investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been instances where the Police have applied to Court for an earlier mention date when investigations are completed, before the end of the remand period.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Minister raised the subject of the setting up of an office of an ombudsman.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the light of this case, I would like to ask Minister whether he thinks this is still appropriate because I noticed that in this particular case, whilst there is no need to doubt the agencies, many are working in silos.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And the agencies are respectively doing investigations on their own personnel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, I am tempted to give the same answer I gave to Mr Leong earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In any event, Sir, there are different parts to this question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I recommended it or I suggested it many years ago.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is something I think Mr Singh has asked me more than once or at least once.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think I have given an answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question is: today, we have done an investigation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What are the different parts to the system?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is the Police, there is AGC, we have given an accounting, there is the State Courts, which we will not expect an accounting from.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is something for the Chief Justice to deal with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think anybody is suggesting any kind of bias.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is full accounting – the key question Members have to ask is what was there before the Police and AGC?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The case in accordance with the usual principles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An ombudsman would do what we would have done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question is whether the ombudsman takes you further for good governance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am happy at some other point to deal with that issue and share examples from different countries how an ombudsman has worked or has not worked and how expectations are set very high and then they are not fulfilled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether we have a functioning Government with integrity and a civil service and a public service that acts with integrity, that is capable of being questioned here and outside, and is prepared to answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How is governance improved by having any other institution?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, those are the questions, but those are larger questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am dealing with a narrower question of what happened in this case in my Statement.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have two points of clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, the Minister has spoken about the evidence in this case in detail and also touched on the findings of further investigations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The second question is, the case was originally seen as one involving a wealthy complainant, fixing their foreign domestic worker, but it seems now that the case is really about wealthy people who are cavalier in dealing with a foreign domestic worker who had, on her part, not exactly acted well as well.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister what is his view on this issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is a very stark question: is Ms Liyani guilty?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She has been acquitted by the High Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said that we must proceed on that basis and not reopen that issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We leave it at that and I do not want to be commenting on the decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to the word "cavalier", the description was not used by me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, on the conduct of the Liews, how you characterise it, I have put across the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think I can usefully add further to those characterisations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this is not rocket science and I think Members can draw their own conclusions as well based on the facts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, I have two clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, Part 1 of his speech went through rather quickly and we were all trying to follow without the Annexes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I think it is important for him to clarify, at the risk of repeating himself, what exactly he is saying about the High Court judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the first point about the High Court, what I said is that the High Court's decision is on the facts before it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am here, I am making a Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I have to set it out in all good faith and honesty and transparency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is all that I am doing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not, in any way, therefore suggesting that if this information was there before the High Court, it could have come to a different decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not want to be making those comments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not the High Court Judge and how can I say, "Oh, if this information was there with him, he would have changed his mind." I can say to you this is the information there is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am being very careful about how I have put it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Ms Sylvia Lim or any Members think that the High Court would have benefited from this information, that is your prerogative for you to think that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I do not think I should be suggesting that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You may think that it would have made no difference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we are just laying out the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is important for me is to show what the Police and AGC had and I am happy for Ms Sylvia Lim's confirmation that there was no expressed influence by LML or his family.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the question is, was there some implicit thinking in the back of his mind?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a question that has struck me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Did the officer, say, think to himself, "This is such a big man, I had better do certain things." If that is the theory, let us look at his conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why did he wait for five weeks then?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do we think that if he was so concerned, "Hey, I better do this properly", then would he have waited for five weeks?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Ms Sylvia Lim may be collapsing two different points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, in good faith and honesty, I am just putting the facts across as an explanation rather than an excuse as to what happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The time taken to visit the scene is different from why he did not seize the items.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regard why he did not seize the items, I have given an explanation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police make a decision as to whether to seize or not to seize.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends on the facts and the nature of the items and assessment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a photograph is adequate, then the officer can decide that he will take a photograph.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These items, they say there is prima facie.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I take photographs and once I have taken the photographs, why do I need the physical items?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is what is meant by "I did not want to re-victimise".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Ms Sylvia Lim may recall that I said, that we should have taken colour photographs, and the way the photographs were taken should have been clearer, item by item.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They should have taken each item and photographed them separately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of that was not done for the clothes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I will give another example why this has got to be a case-by-case thing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was a one matter that came to me as a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were in the trade – they deal with gold.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The gold that they were dealing with was said to be the subject of fraud.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And therefore, the Police, at that time, seized the entire amount of gold which was quite substantial and they were investigating the alleged fraudsters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The people who claimed ownership of the gold – and I think there was no doubt that they are entitled to the gold – came to see me to say, "Meanwhile the prices are oscillating, they are going up, they are going down and the Police are holding on to the gold.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can we not please be subjected to this?" And it did go up, quite substantially.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you got to assess on the case whether here do I need to seize or do I need to take a photograph.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, in relation to the investigation by the investigating officer or IO at Tanglin Police Division, I understand that it was classified as a routine theft case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder whether given the factual complexities, as opposed to the legal complexities, the Police could approach this in a different way, in future, so that the necessary expertise may be borne onto the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I know that that is how the private sector does it – you come in quickly, the lawyers come in, and aid and help the people who are doing the investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the second point that he has made about the Judicial Service Commission.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Notice of Motion.
